Succor
SUK-er
v. or n.
From Old French sucurre, from Latin succurrere, “to run beneath, run to help,” from sub- (under) + currere (to run). The picture is literal: to run beneath or alongside as help. Renders the Greek boētheō, “to help,” and antilambanō, “to take hold of, support.”

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Succor in the KJV is the antique English verb for to help, aid, run to one’s assistance—a word whose Latin etymology (sub- + currere, to run beneath) captures the picture of literal coming-alongside-with-help. The verb’s most theologically weighty NT use is in the high-priestly application to Christ in Hebrews 2:18: for in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted. The Greek boētheō means to run to help upon a cry; Christ’s qualification to succor the tempted is precisely that He Himself was tempted, suffered being tempted, and now stands ready to come to the aid of His people in their parallel trials. The verb has its OT-narrative uses also. The Syro-Phoenician woman’s cry to Christ for her daughter: Lord, help me—in the KJV often rendered with the succoring picture (Matt 15:25). Paul’s commendation of Phebe to the Romans: that ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also (Rom 16:1-2). The biblical doctrine of succor therefore has two principal applications. Christologically, Christ Himself succors the tempted—He hears the cry of His people under trial, runs to their assistance, and brings the help they need precisely because He has been tempted Himself and knows the weight. Ecclesiologically, the saints succor one another—Phebe’s succor of many and of Paul himself is a Pauline model, and the church saturated with such mutual succor is the church living out the body-of-Christ identity in concrete embodied care. The recovery of the word is therefore the recovery of two doctrines: the high-priestly succor of Christ to His tempted people, and the mutual succor of saints to one another in the body. Both belong together. Christ succors the tempted; His saints, taught of Him, succor one another in turn.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SUCCOR as to run to, or run to support; hence, to help or relieve when in difficulty, want or distress; to assist and deliver from suffering; in scripture, the verb of Christ’s high-priestly aid to the tempted and of the saints’ mutual aid in the body.

expand to see more

SUCCOR, v.t. — To run to, or run to support; hence, to help or relieve when in difficulty, want or distress; to assist and deliver from suffering. He is able to succour them that are tempted (Heb 2:18).

SUCCOR, n. — Aid; help; assistance; particularly assistance that relieves and delivers from difficulty, want or distress. For she hath been a succourer of many (Rom 16:2).

📖 Key Scripture

Hebrews 2:18 — "For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted."

2 Corinthians 6:2 — "...behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation."

Romans 16:1-2 — "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also."

Matthew 15:25 — "Then came she and worshipped him, saying, Lord, help me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Succor is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by retaining a word that has nearly dropped from modern usage; the loss in modern translations is the loss of the picture-in-the-etymology of running-beneath-with-help that suits both Christ’s high-priestly aid to the tempted and the saints’ mutual aid in the body.

expand to see more

Succor has nearly dropped from modern English usage, surviving chiefly in literary and military contexts. Modern translations replace it with help, aid, or rephrase the construction. The substitution is grammatically defensible; the loss is in the picture the etymology supplies. Succor—literally to run beneath, run to assist—captures the action of help in motion, the picture of running to one’s side when the cry goes up, the urgency of help applied to the moment of need. Help in modern usage is more static and abstract; succor still carries the picture of the runner arriving with what is needed. The KJV’s retention of the word preserves both the picture and the register.

The doctrine the word supports is also worth recovering. Christ’s high-priestly succor (Heb 2:18) is one of the most pastorally tender doctrines of the New Testament: the One who runs to the aid of His tempted people is qualified to do so precisely because He has been tempted Himself, has suffered being tempted, and brings to the help He renders the deep sympathy of one who knows the weight. The believer in temptation is therefore not merely sympathized with by a distant deity but actively succored by an experienced high priest who runs to His side. And the church’s mutual succor (Phebe, Rom 16:2) is patterned on Christ’s own: saints running to the aid of fellow-saints in need, the body-of-Christ ministry rendered concrete in the practical care of brothers and sisters in their actual distresses. Recover the word, recover the doctrine, and recover the practice: Christ’s succor to the tempted, and the saints’ succor to one another, are both meant to fill the contemporary church as they filled the apostolic one.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin succurrere (to run beneath, run to help) from sub- + currere; renders Greek boētheō (to help upon a cry) and antilambanō (to take hold of, support)—the picture of running-to-help, applied to Christ’s high-priestly aid to the tempted and the saints’ mutual aid in the body.

expand to see more

Latin succurrere — to run beneath, run to help (the etymological root).

Greek boētheō (G997) — to help upon a cry (Heb 2:18; Matt 15:25; Mark 9:22, 24; Acts 16:9; 21:28; 2 Cor 6:2; Rev 12:16).

Greek antilēmptōr (G484) — one who takes hold of, helper, succorer.

Greek prostatis (G4368) — a female protector, helper, succorer (Rom 16:2 of Phebe).

Usage

"He is able to succour them that are tempted—Christ’s high-priestly qualification to run to the aid of His tempted people, grounded in His own temptation and suffering."

"Phebe, a succourer of many, and of myself also—Pauline model of the saint’s mutual succor in the body of Christ."

"Succor captures the picture of running-with-help that help in modern usage has flattened; the older verb names both Christ’s high-priestly aid and the saints’ embodied mutual care."
